content: It remains uncertain whether the use of iron-chelating agents, such as intravenous desferrioxamine (DFO) or oral deferiprone, either as standalone treatments or in combination with standard antimalarial therapies, can effectively reduce mortality in malaria patients. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of iron-chelating agents, alone or in conjunction with standard antimalarial drugs, for the treatment of Plasmodium falciparum malaria. A comprehensive search was conducted in May 2007 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and mRCT. Reference lists were also reviewed, and researchers in the field were contacted to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials that compared iron-chelating agents with placebo or iron-chelating agents combined with standard antimalarial drugs versus antimalarial drugs alone, in both adult and pediatric populations with P. falciparum malaria. The methodological quality of the trials was independently assessed, and data extraction was performed by one author. Additional data were sought from trial authors. Dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RR), while continuous outcomes were analyzed using weighted mean differences (MD), both presented with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Seven trials, involving a total of 570 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Two small trials compared DFO with placebo, with both groups receiving standard antimalarial drugs. These trials did not provide evidence of either benefit or harm in terms of mortality, but the sample size was limited (435 participants). However, one trial (334 participants) demonstrated a reduced risk of persistent seizures in the DFO group compared to placebo (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.95). Despite this, adverse effects were more frequently observed in participants receiving DFO. Another small trial, involving 45 adults and children, compared deferiprone with placebo, with both groups also receiving standard antimalarial drugs. In this trial, participants treated with deferiprone experienced significantly faster recovery from coma (MD -27 hours, 95% CI -34.20 to -19.80) and faster parasite clearance (MD -24 hours, 95% CI -35.27 to -12.73). Notably, no adverse effects were reported in this trial. The authors concluded that the available data are insufficient to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of DFO and deferiprone in the treatment of P. falciparum malaria. While there was a nonsignificant trend toward fewer seizures with DFO, this was accompanied by an overall increase in adverse effects, including mortality. Results from the single small trial of deferiprone suggest potential benefits in terms of faster coma recovery and parasite clearance, but the evidence is limited. As of 2008, the authors decided not to update this review due to the scarcity of recent trials in this area and shifting research priorities in malaria treatment.
